reference_books.title: Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail
reference_books.review_text: I couldn't bond with Cheryl Strayed despite having lost my mother early as well. There didn't seem to be any big revelations other than she didn't feel the need to sleep with as many men afterward and I didn't see the correlation. There seemed to be a lot of focus on how the men hikers were enthralled with her. I wasn't. I have no desire to hike the Pacific Crest Trail partly because I didn't before hand and she didn't make it seem the least bit fun or enlightening.

reference_books.title: The Girl on the Train
reference_books.review_text: Read this book in two long evenings. I couldn't put it down. There isn't a single likable character in this book, all of their lives are train wrecks that you can't help but gawk at. The comparisons to Gone Girl are good. This is a great debut novel.

reference_books.title: Murder on the Orient Express (Hercule Poirot, #10)
reference_books.review_text: This was fun and nostalgic for me. I read many of these Agatha Christie books as a kid, and wanted to revisit this one because of the upcoming film adaptation.

reference_books.title: In the Garden of Beasts: Love, Terror, and an American Family in Hitler's Berlin
reference_books.review_text: 3.5 stars. I liked it a lot. It was a fresh take on the horrors of Nazi Germany including American complacency in some of it.

reference_books.title: The Moviegoer
reference_books.review_text: I was sure I'd love this book, maybe that's what went wrong for me. The subject and the setting seemed right up my alley but I couldn't relate to the main character at all. I tried and tried to finish it put couldn't and it's only 240 pages. Maybe someday I'll try again from scratch with lower expectations, or at least not expecting to see any part of me in Binx

book_a.title: Heft
book_a.user_review: I loved this book. I thought it would be hard to relate to a 500 pound shut in but it wasn't. We all have different ways of coping with the weight of our past and there are usually some good reasons for why people are the way they are. I could relate to all of the characters especially Kel, the teenager, who always had lots of friends but never really felt like he fit in. Very well written. It keeps you interested and curious and the ending was quietly inspirational.

sample_reviews.review_text: Can't seem to get into it.

Full disclosure: my boyfriend met Liz Moore at a film screening a few years ago, and his ongoing acquaintanceship with her (which included the three of us having lunch together one day this summer) is what prompted me to check this book out from the library--I'm not sure I would ever have found it otherwise. And even if I had found it, I'm not sure if the flap copy would have inspired me to read it: the description of the book as a "memorable, heartbreaking, and ultimately redemptive novel about finding sustenance and friendship in the most surprising places" made me fear it would be sentimental. But my boyfriend said he thought I'd like it, and he knows my taste pretty well. Sure enough: I liked this book a whole lot. 
 Heft is narrated in part by Arthur Opp, a former academic who guesses he weighs between 500 and 600 pounds and who hasn't left his Brooklyn home for ten years (since 9/11), and in part by Kel Keller, the teenage son of a former student of Arthur's named Charlene. The very start of the book is a letter Arthur starts writing to Charlene, telling her about his current life and apologizing for what he's omitted to tell her in the previous letters he's written to her (his weight, his lack of a job, his reclusive state): it's prompted by a phone call he got from her three days earlier, in which she said she would send him a letter. The letter, though, turns out not to be a letter at all: it's a photograph of Kel, which is then followed by another phone call from Charlene. Kel needs help with college applications, Charlene says: all he thinks about is baseball. Charlene suggests that she and Kel could visit Arthur, a possibility that's exciting and worrying to him: no one's been in his house in seven years. So he hires a cleaning service, and a maid named Yolanda arrives, and her presence in Arthur's life is better for him than he expected: she doesn't just clean, she's someone to talk with; she's someone who can convince him to talk, and who will listen. 
 Kel, meanwhile, lives in Yonkers but goes to school in a wealthier suburb where his mom used to work; he's basically raising himself as best he can because his dad left when he was four, and his mom is dealing with problems of her own (she also, it seems, does not really leave the house). Kel is athletic and popular but also lonely; he's a kid from a poor neighborhood who goes to a school of privileged kids, and he's aware of his difference. He likes baseball and is very good at it; he thinks maybe baseball will be what changes his life and his mom's life, if he can get into the majors instead of going to college. 
 Things happen, and it's hard to say anything about any of them without being spoiler-y (while this is largely a character-driven book, it's also a plot-driven book), and people write letters and read letters and are lonely, or have moments of connection, or both. I like the way this book is written, the occasional formality of Arthur's voice and the ease of Kel's, and the details that make each of those voices feel right, like when Kel is driving down a pretty street and there's this: "There's a horse farm to my right and I watch a woman open and close a fence behind her and call to one of them. The blanketed horse comes to her and she clips a leash-thing onto his face-thing and then the two of them walk toward the barn" (208). I also really liked the ending (like, so much so that I read it and then stopped and handed the book to my boyfriend and told him to read the last paragraph, because it felt so good and right), though if reviews on Goodreads are representative, I am apparently in the minority--a lot of people apparently really hated the end. (It's an inconclusive ending, which felt right to me for the book and for the characters: it ends at a threshold, with possibility and uncertainty, rather than with some climactic scene.)

I really enjoyed the voices in this novel, especially at the onset. I would have given it 4 stars except that I felt a little robbed of a pay off at the end. This novel is what I like to call a fill-in-the-blanker because it leaves the moment you've been waiting for the entire time up to your own imagination. There are obvious plusses (leave them wanting more) and minuses (leave us wanting more) to this approach. This time I was a bit annoyed. But a worthy read nonetheless.
Teenage boys who live for baseball and fail English do not sound like 30-something-year-old women with MFA's in creative writing.
Started this book VERY skeptically ... Turns out .. LOVED IT !!! Amazing character development , a book you just won't be able to put down

This started out pretty good for me. I enjoyed reading about Arthur and Kel and finding out how they were connected. The story was building toward the end and then...nothing. I was very disappointed with the ending, or lack thereof. I didn't feel like either one of them changed, so what is the point of the book?

I loved HEFT. Wonderful writing; great, nuanced characters. The novel is easy to get into, yet truly thought-provoking. I guess you could say it's got heft. Moore has done a lovely job exploring the nature of loneliness, and the lengths we will go to to connect or to avoid connecting. Read it!

Very gripping in the beginning. I love the concept of this story. interesting to view the circumstances through the eyes of a person with an eating addiction. Some of this story was a but run-on. I think that the ending could have been written a bit better. I did enjoy this one.

Because of the structure of the novel, I feel that I could give one rating to Arthur's section (two stars) and another to Kel's (four stars). I did not connect or really ever care about Arthur (and was generally annoyed with the use of the "&" throughout his section). Kel's section was like reading a good young adult novel, which is not a criticism because I love a good YA read. There was a poignancy and some suspense in Kel's story that wasn't there for me with Arthur.
Forced; it required that I suspend disbelief on multiple fronts. The ending felt like one too many deadlines had been missed and the book had to be abruptly finished.

book_b.title: Life
book_b.user_review:
A must read for Stones fans, and a fun read for anyone who likes rock and roll. There are lots of interesting tidbits including, creating creative interesting sounds with low-fi, seeing where some lyrics came from and understanding Keith's rocky relationship with Mick. 
 Keith is certainly an interesting character. This book shows that there's more to him than meets the eye. Even with the sex, drugs, & rock n roll, he's quite a romantic. Relationships are very important to him despite the fact that he screwed many of them up with drug abuse. 
 Also, for anyone beating themselves up about what you may have done wrong as a parent, when you see how Keith was raised versus how his son was raised, and how each of them turned out, you might be a little easier on yourself.

sample_reviews.review_text:
By Keith Richards 
 Back Bay Books 576 pgs 
 978-0316034418 
 From my library 
 Rating: 5 - Sheer Perfection 
 Full disclosure: I am hopelessly in love with Keith Richards 
 OK, now that you know that I'd like to talk about rock and roll for a minute. Rock and roll is a force of nature. It can and does work radical change on every culture it touches. Remember back in the day when parents were horrified by it and teachers warned of a break down in discipline and preachers were calling rock and roll the devil's music? Everyone was running around hyperventilating and claiming that this music was all about sex and the ruination of western civilization was at hand. I always thought that claim about sex was utterly ridiculous. But you know what? It is about sex. It's sexy, exciting, feverish, sweaty and little dirty (come on you know it.) Hedonism personified. So is Keith Richards. 
 Mr. Richards is living quite a life and shows no signs of slacking off after some 50 years as a guitarist, vocalist, songwriter and co-founder of the Rolling Stones. He spent his childhood in Dartford, England as an only child. He joined a boys' choir and sang in Westminster Abbey for the queen. Then his voice began to change with puberty and that was all she wrote for that choir. They kicked him out. Keith was devastated. It was a betrayal. And so he turned into a delinquent, sort of, and to this day carries with him a deeply felt contempt for anyone or anything claiming authority. His grandfather Gus gave him a guitar. 
 Keith discovered rock and roll while listening to the radio late at night in his room under the covers because he was supposed to be asleep. "Heartbreak Hotel." Then he began to hunt down rock and roll and it's predecessor, American blues. Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf. He taught himself to play these songs. Then one day he happened into a man on a train platform with a couple of these records under his arm. Mick Jagger. They began to get together to play and Mick knew a couple of other guys and pretty soon they had a band. They played covers of rhythm and blues songs. The Stones played the club circuit where they were very successful. The band had accomplished what Keith and Mick had envisioned: they were a highly successful London rhythm and blues band. Then along came Andrew Oldham. Turns out that old story about his locking Keith and Mick in a kitchen until they came out with a song is true. "As Tears Go By." 
 And then Toad's Wild Ride. 
 Keith's personal relationships have been tumultuous, let's say. A decade long relationship with Anita Pallenberg gave him two children, Marlon and Angela. Another baby died as an infant of CIDS. Keith doesn't say much about that and I wouldn't either. His relationship with Anita finally fell apart due to a devastating heroin addiction. Keith finally got clean and Anita couldn't. A few years later he met and fell in love with Patti Hansen, a model in New York. They have been married for almost 30 years and have two daughters, Theodora and Alexandra. 
 This book is also deeply satisfying. It is candid, the good and the bad, the ugly and the sublime, and as a reader you are grateful for that. Keith is not a tease. My conclusions in the end are that this is a moral man. He knows right and wrong in a cosmic sense. He gives and demands loyalty most of all. And he is a loyal father, son, husband, band mate and friend. In the end the best thing about this book is the style in which it is told. There's a riff behind the words. Life is written as if you were sitting at the kitchen table having a drink, a smoke or two, and telling stories. 
 Please visit the author: http://www.keithrichards.com/ 
 And http://www.rollingstones.com/
Wish I could give this book 6 stars!! What else can I say FANTASTIC!!!!!

Very disappointed. I felt like this was going to be the greatest rock n roll story ever told. I got halfway through it. It just meanders all over his childhood and then some early, but boring, Stones in the US stories. I mean, the most exciting part was when they got arrested in Alabama or LA or AR. In other words, not so exciting.

Slow going in the first half--the story is "spoken" by Keith--obviously to a ghost writer/editor. 
 But I must say by the end of the book, Keith charmed me.
I bailed on it. I decided I don't care as much about the Stones as I thought I did.
Good book. Not a Rolling Stones fan. Read about 1/2 of the book then it started sounding the same. It would probably be really great if you were a fan.

so, i didn't actually finished because my playaway kept dying on me. but i had made it about 4/5 of the way through despite wanting to be done after the first couple of chapters, so whatever. not worth any more time.
made it to page 140 then just looked at the pictures. I really wanted to love it, but couldn't get into it for some reason.

Good ol' fashioned, "confessional-style" autobio that effortlessly shifts from the sublime to the mundane. I liked this much better than Ronnie's book. Kinda wish the publisher woulda included a glossory or footnotes to explain what some of his regional/generational colloquialisms(?) are. Loved following the trajectory of his relationship with Mick. Felt a little like a Greek tragedy. Also liked when he turned to friends to give first hand personal accounts of certain events. I was bugged by some things he seems to have included to pad out some chapters. It felt like he sat down and just thought to himself "Hmmm, now-what do I feel like writing about today" How he found his cat (and dog), recipe for bangers and mash, and the name dropping of people in his "inner circle" seemed a little contrived. Fans of Keith will love this although those who have been following him over the years are probably familiar with many of the road stories included here.

Keith Richards is a sound, and listening to the first few licks of "Gimme Shelter" should demonstrate this. 
 I recognise that I'm the wrong generation to speak about the "legend" that is Keith Richards, but I've always been a man out of time when it comes to music. My parents grew me up on AC DC and Aerosmith, and after I discovered Guns N Roses I eventually stumbled onto the Rolling Stones which remain one of my favorite rock bands of all time. Keith Richards especially has remained this kind of mythic figure to me, but NOT because the man did drugs in the seventies. Keith Richards is an incredible man to me for the way his music has helped shape so many musicians who in turn have contributed so much to culture. 
 Life, as a book, is nothing like what I was used to with rock biographies. While most deal with drug abuse, a fall from grace, and then an eventual return to rock god-dom, Richards's book really just tackles the man's life which has been contumacious. The man has lived a life that is entirely his own, and even his worst blunders were mistakes which he owned and lived because they were his choices. 
 But the reason the reader should take the time to read this book, or at least listen to the audio-book like I did (Johnney Depp and Joe Hurley read everything until Richards takes over at the last chapter), is because the book is not just an effort to record the facts. Richards raps the events of his life as if he's speaking one on one with his reader, and as they hear the events of Altamont, his struggles with Mick Jagger and Anita Pallenburg, or the famous fall from the tree, it never feels that Richards is trying to oversell, or defend himself. He is, as always, just giving what is actually him. There's a power in that, while reading, and it bleeds onto the reader so that finishing this book, you can almost hear the blues in your bones. 
 Can't recommend it enough.
